body: Could we rather move all the conditionals to [`createSendEventForHits()`](https://github.com/algolia/instantsearch.js/blob/0a517609de103eef4f8edfefe6e28a1d79a14209/src/lib/utils/createSendEventForHits.ts#L150)?

Would it make sense here? I'm not convinced that a function responsible for transformation should also take global state in account: 

https://github.com/algolia/instantsearch.js/blob/99f6fe1dc51e4815e5b9efcfb30e3e2f3127e763/src/lib/utils/createSendEventForHits.ts#L91-L104

Also note that the sendEvent function can be called by end users. I'm not sure if we then also should prevent forwarding the event if the search is currently stalled

I thought about having a short circuit before this line: https://github.com/algolia/instantsearch.js/blob/99f6fe1dc51e4815e5b9efcfb30e3e2f3127e763/src/lib/utils/createSendEventForHits.ts#L159

But I don't have the complete knowledge of this part.

> Also note that the sendEvent function can be called by end users. I'm not sure if we then also should prevent forwarding the event if the search is currently stalled

I think the question is: should it send an event when the search is stalled?

I don't think it should because (IIUC):

1. a render displays hits: send view event
2. user searches
3. a render displays hits again because search is stalled: ~send view event~

And so I don't think this (3) makes sense.

if we do this condition only for `view` event I agree, but if it should be all events that get shortcutted I don't think so, because you could be in a stalled state, but click on a buy button, that's a genuine action which should count right?

Before the line you mentioned wouldn't work, as sendEvent only gets created once, but right underneath could, with the caveat the condition exists for every type of event, not just view

I think it makes sense to have guards per event type centralized in `createSendEventForHits`. For now we can have only one for `view` since we have knowledge about when it should and should not be sent, we don't need to guard for all events.

Could we make a higher-level test that makes use of [`stalledSearchDelay`](https://www.algolia.com/doc/api-reference/widgets/instantsearch/js/#widget-param-stalledsearchdelay) and a search client mock that resolves after this time?

The test would be easier to understand, and more resilient over time.

I guess that's possible, but other tests relying on timing are the ones which are flaky (routing, answers debouncing). I originally manually rendered setting the searchMetadata, but the way this test is written was resilient with moving the implementation from render args to InstantSearch._isSearchStalled. 

Unless you're maybe suggesting a search client which never resolves?

Yes, that could also work.

What bothers me in this test is that it interacts with deep internals and doesn't completely reflect the user scenario.

solved with a "dead" search client in https://github.com/algolia/instantsearch.js/pull/5058/commits/7131b4a1b67ee37b0317e4531fdfec40ee121793

Thanks for the idea!
Are these fake timers? Otherwise we can decrease this amount with `stalledSearchDelay`.
had to add a margin, probably due to timers being "minimal", and them allowing to overtake eachother
this is false, because if the search is stalled, you still want to bind events (for later)
